narrative:
The model estimated your chance of bad credit at 38%, meaning that roughly 38 out of 100 applicants with a similar profile would be expected not to repay as agreed. That risk was high enough under the lender’s rules for denial, although it is not a certainty; the remaining 62% reflects possible good repayment.

The strongest reason was your checking-account status: it was overdrawn, below zero. This was the most influential factor and pushed the decision toward bad credit. Only about 12.6% of approved applicants had this status, compared with 59.2% with no account, so it stood out as unusual and risky.

Two other factors worked in your favour but did not outweigh that concern. Your savings position—no known savings—was the second most important factor and pushed toward good credit in your case, even though many approved applicants had small balances. Your stated purpose, “other,” was third and also pushed toward good credit; it is less common than radio/TV or furniture loans but was not treated as a negative signal.

To improve a future application, ask the lender to confirm the checking-account information is accurate, bring the account into a positive balance, and provide recent statements. Strengthening savings and, if possible, applying for a smaller amount or adding a suitable guarantor may also help. Reapply only when these points can be documented.
